title: Password manager fundamentals
body_md:
## One tool that ends most credential attacks

A password manager is software that remembers every login for you, in an encrypted vault that only you can unlock. That's it. The mechanism is plain. The defensive consequences are enormous.

### What a manager actually does

- **Generates** a unique random password for every new account you create (typically 20+ characters, uniform random).
- **Stores** every password in a single encrypted file (your vault).
- **Auto-fills** the right credentials on the right domain. If the domain doesn't match, it refuses to fill — which doubles as a phishing detector.
- **Syncs** the vault across your devices, so you have access on phone, laptop, browser.

The single point of failure is the *master password* you use to unlock the vault. That one password you do need to remember, and it should be a long passphrase you've never used anywhere else.

### What the manager protects against

| Attack | Protection |
|---|---|
| Credential stuffing | Every password is unique. A breach of one service can't reach others. |
| Phishing | Auto-fill won't run on a wrong domain. The manager refuses to suggest your bank credentials on a fake bank page. |
| Weak passwords | Generated passwords resist offline cracking for centuries. |
| Forgetting | The vault remembers; you don't have to. |

### What the manager does *not* protect against

- **Malware on your device.** Once an attacker controls the device, they can keystroke-log your master password or read your vault directly. Keep device security up first.
- **Master-password phishing.** If someone tricks you into typing your master password into a fake interface, the game's over. Most modern managers will refuse to recognize lookalike URLs — but be careful around the master password.

### Choosing one

Reputable options as of 2025: **1Password**, **Bitwarden** (free tier is fine), **Apple Passwords** (built into iCloud Keychain), **Proton Pass**. Any of these is hugely better than no manager. Avoid:

- Random unknown apps from third-party app stores.
- Browser-only autofill *without* a master password (less secure).
- The 'remember password' option in shared/family computers.

### Getting started — a 30-minute migration plan

1. Install a password manager and create one strong, long master passphrase.
2. Walk through your browser's saved passwords. Import them into the vault. Delete from the browser.
3. For your top 10 highest-value accounts (email, bank, social, work), rotate the password to a manager-generated one.
4. Over the next two weeks, rotate the rest as you log in.

This is the single highest-leverage half-hour you can spend on personal security.

widget_config.setup: You just installed Bitwarden and finished setting your master passphrase. The next time you open Amazon to make a purchase, the autofill icon doesn't appear on the password field. You're sure you saved this account in the vault.

choices.text: The vault is broken — fall back to typing the password from memory.
choices.explanation: Reaching for memorized passwords trains the wrong habit. The whole value of the manager is that you stop knowing your passwords. Investigate before you fall back.

choices.text: Check the address bar — the page might be on a domain that doesn't match the saved entry (real Amazon vs. fake Amazon).
choices.explanation: Correct. A no-autofill on a familiar-looking page is the manager's phishing detector firing. Check the URL. If the registered domain isn't amazon.com, the page is fake and you just got saved from typing into a credential-harvest form.

choices.text: Disable the manager so it stops being annoying.
choices.explanation: You'd be turning off the single best phishing detector you have. The no-autofill behaviour is doing its job; don't dismantle it.

widget_config.moral: Treat your password manager's refusals as security signals, not annoyances.
